newsitem.title: USA: NEWT GINGRICH: fateful day for political battler.
newsitem.headline: NEWT GINGRICH: fateful day for political battler.

text.p: Two turbulent years at the pinnacle of power have transformed House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich from conquering political hero with doubled fists to a man with hat in hand, seeking survival.

Humbled by ethical breaches now hanging over his head and scarred too by political blunders, the 53-year-old conservative Georgian with the muffin face and ink-dot eyes beloved of political cartoonists, was reduced on Tuesday to soliciting once-obedient party colleagues for the support he needs to be re-elected speaker in a make-or-break House vote.

Whatever the outcome, It was a far cry from the cocky, combative political pit bull who took the speakership by right two years ago as architect of an election triumph that gave Republicans their first congressional majorities in 40 years.

He was chosen as Time magazine's "Man of the Year" cover boy. He was much discussed as a potential 1996 Republican presidential candidate. He was, as his supporters loved to chant on sight of him, "Newt! Newt! Newt!"

He remains a political force, able and shrewd. But it is an admittedly sadder, undoubtedly wiser Newt Gingrich now trying to hold onto the third-highest elective office in the United States after the presidency and vice presidency.

Even if he succeeded in his quest to become the first Republican elected speaker in successive Congresses since 1929, he would also become -- in about two weeks, after House disciplinary procedures that begin on Wednesday -- the first speaker ever to face punishment by vote of the House.

The immediate cause of Gingrich's woes are the findings of a House ethics subcommittee -- which he has conceded "with great sadness" -- that he failed to prevent the improper use of tax-exempt funds to finance a lecture series he conducted, and that he misled House investigators about this.
It seemed likely he would face later this month at least official reprimand, the third most severe penalty available.
And this is only the latest of his problems.

His often harsh pursuit of conservative Republican reform proposals -- many embedded in a so-called "Contract with America" -- enabled Democrats to demonise him in this year's election campaign as a heartless elitist who wanted to slash Medicare health insurance for the elderly and disabled.
Some Republicans shunned him in their own campaigns.

The Medicare attacks and two partial shutdowns of the U.S. government in a budget dispute with President Bill Clinton last winter, for which many voters blamed the Republicans, hurt Republicans in the election and reduced their House majority to 227 to 207 for the Democrats, and one independent.

As a result an unusually chastened Gingrich has adopted a more conciliatory political stance and has effectively ceded much of his high-profile leadership role to Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, an old, congenial ally.

"I want to suggest to you that if the last Congress was the confrontation Congress, this Congress will be the implementation Congress," Gingrich told Republicans who renominated him for the speakership last fall.

And only on Monday, before leaving Georgia to return to Washington and fight for re-election, he forecast a brave new world of accord between him and Clinton, Republicans and Democrats on key issues like budget-balancing and tax cuts.

"The president basically broadly agrees," he said of the man he once disdainfully dismissing as "the enemy of normal people." He added: "I think we're at the edge here of potentially a brand new large coalition."

That from an 18-year congressman who has made his name as a House "bomb-thrower" and ethics warrior since he entered the House in 1978. He helped to force the resignation of Democratic Speaker Jim Wright on ethics charges in 1989, a feat many Democrats have never forgotten or forgiven.

With fame as speaker since 1995 has come his own heavy doses of controversy. First came his acceptance of a $4.5 million advance for his book, "To Renew America." He bowed to widespread criticism and turned down the advance.
And Democrats who recall his protrayals of Congress as "corrupt" under their rule and his role in Wright's downfall have filed many ethics complaints against him.
Most were dismissed, some led to letters of mild rebuke, and two are the foundation of his current problems.
Gingrich was born June 17, 1943, in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. He is married and has two grown daughters from a first marriage that ended in divorce.
